ai.base_rate_used: Scenario page base rate: 0 downgrades in 36 recorded S&P actions on EU sovereigns with a stable outlook going in (0%, and 0% as a lower bound on the wider count). S&P usually moves the outlook to negative before it cuts, so I start near zero and allow a small tail for an off-pattern cut.

factors.text: The reference class is clean on this point. S&P has not cut any of these six EU sovereigns straight from a stable outlook since 2014. The normal path is an outlook change first, and an outlook change alone resolves NO. This is the main reason I sit well below the market.

The fiscal and political backdrop is getting worse, which gives S&P cover to act. HCFP calls the 1.0% growth forecast optimistic and sees debt rising toward about 122%. Budget adoption by 31 December is close to a coin flip (50.5% and 49%). Marine Le Pen is priced at 41.1% to win in 2027. The OAT-Bund spread widened from 81.5bp to 96.7bp on the monthly series. This mostly argues for a negative outlook, but it keeps a direct cut possible.

Where the crowd may share an error: the 26.5% Polymarket price trades on thin volume (7345). The 31% Kalshi contract covers any agency through year-end, so it is wider than this question. Both seem to treat a bad fiscal story as if it meant an S&P cut on 27 Nov, and skip the outlook-first habit. The spread series is a degraded monthly average, and no gauge here is tested as a lead on rating actions.

ai.what_would_change_view: Any of these before 27 Nov would push me up toward the market: the government falls on a censure motion, PLF 2027 is rejected at first reading so a special law becomes the base case, or the government raises its 2026 deficit estimate. A confirmation that S&P's current outlook is already negative, not stable, would also break the reference class. A quiet first reading with the revenue part passed would push me toward affirm_stable.
ai.most_likely_wrong: The 'stable outlook going in' premise could be wrong, or S&P could decide that political paralysis before the 2027 election justifies an off-pattern cut. In either case the 0% reference class does not apply and the market's roughly one-in-four is closer to right.

ai.base_rate_used: The scenario page gives 19 of 21 budgets promulgated by 31 December (90.5%) across 2006-2026. I give more weight to the subset since France lost its majority in 2022. The page shows that subset separately but does not quote it. Its branch notes say the 2024 and 2025 cycles both ended with a special law. The most relevant starting point is therefore roughly a coin flip for a minority government, well below 90.5%.

factors.text: Structural: a minority government since the 2024 dissolution. The last two budget cycles both missed 31 December and ended with a special law, the 2024 and 2025 pattern noted on the scenario page. The full-sample base rate of 90.5% mostly comes from years with a majority.

This budget is politically harder than usual. It has about 54 billion euros of consolidation, including a freeze of basic pensions and of the civil-service pay index. It lands just before the spring 2027 presidential race, in which Le Pen has launched her campaign and is priced at 41.1%. Opposition parties gain little from letting it pass, and a 49.3 invites a censure vote.

The government has tools to force it through. Kalshi prices use of Article 49.3 on the budget in 2026 at 66%. The Article 47 deadline of 10 December also opens a never-used ordinance route. This keeps the chance of adoption well above zero, provided the government survives.

ai.what_would_change_view: I would move up if PS or LR publicly commit not to censure a 49.3 text, or if a joint committee agreement is reached in mid-December. I would move down if a censure motion gathers PS votes, if the revenue part fails at first reading in November, or if the government signals a special law as in 2024 and 2025.
ai.most_likely_wrong: Prediction markets at 50.5% and 49% may be right. The government may have secured a quiet non-censure deal, like the one that eventually passed the 2026 budget, and simply land it before Christmas this time, given the reputational cost of a third consecutive special law. My pre-election pessimism could then be overdone. The market signals themselves carry little tested evidence, and the official-optimism gauge is untested.

ai.base_rate_used: The scenario page has no computed probability for an RN win. Its reference class says the final-poll leader won 4 of 4 presidential run-offs, with an RMS poll error of 5.78 pp. That only helps once final polls exist, and the snapshot holds no polls six months out. As a last resort I start from market prices: on Polymarket, Le Pen at 41.1% plus Bardella at 1.7%; on Kalshi, Le Pen at 45% plus Bardella at 1.4%. Together that puts the RN candidate in the low-to-mid 40s.

factors.text: Markets price the RN candidate highest among single candidates. Le Pen has formally launched her campaign, and headlines are framing the race as hers to lose. That keeps the starting point near the market level. Note that the market splits RN odds between Le Pen and Bardella as though her ineligibility case were mostly settled; the question counts either name, so that split does not change the YES side.

The centre-right side is split across Lisnard at 19.6%, Philippe at 14.5%, Lagarde at 4.2% and others, and together they are close to the RN total. A run-off is usually a two-way race in which non-RN voters consolidate, and the signposts say that consolidation (withdrawals, sponsorship totals in March 2027) has not happened yet. I shade slightly below the market because fragmented anti-RN odds tend to understate the eventual run-off opponent.

The crowd's main gauge carries little evidential weight. The poll-versus-prediction-market gap is badged tested_no_lead, and prediction-market series in general are tested_no_lead. These markets have high volume but are untested as forecasters this far out. Fiscal strain could still feed the anti-incumbent vote: HCFP expects debt to rise toward about 122% of GDP and sees the 2029 deficit target as very unlikely to be met.

ai.what_would_change_view: I would move up if second-round polls against the leading centre-right candidate show RN ahead by more than the 5.78 pp historical poll error, or if the centre-right stays split into March 2027. I would move down if one centre-right candidate consolidates (the others withdraw) and run-off polls show RN behind. A ruling that keeps Le Pen off the ballot would matter only if Bardella polled weaker than her.
ai.most_likely_wrong: I may be underrating RN. The old pattern of anti-RN voters uniting in the run-off may have weakened enough, under fiscal austerity and a polarised climate, that the market's low-to-mid 40s is too low rather than too high.

ai.base_rate_used: The scenario page has no computed base rate; em-macro records no Brazilian fiscal-target revisions. My starting point is the page's context: Brazil cut a self-set primary target in July 2015 (mid-year, under fiscal stress) and in April 2024 (the following year's target, inside the PLDO). That suggests revisions are a real risk, but they usually come with the April budget-guidelines cycle, after this question's 31 March window closes. I start near 70% that the target and rule survive to 31 March.

factors.text: The government's own 2027 budget bill says the framework is met. It shows a counted surplus of R$83.4 billion against a R$73.2 billion target, and the target has a tolerance band of 0.25 point of GDP either side. A re-elected government entering its new term on 5 January has little reason to formally cut a target it claims to be meeting within its first three months. The more natural place to move goalposts is the April budget-guidelines cycle, which falls outside the window.

Independent estimates sit far from the target. IFI puts the counted 2027 result at only R$0.9 billion, below even the lower tolerance bound, and says about R$35.7 billion of spending would have to be frozen. IFI also sees a potential 2027 deficit of 1.0% of GDP. The Focus 2027 median is -0.3% of GDP against the 0.5% target, though that dispersion gauge is untested. A spending freeze of that size early in a new term is politically hard, so the first bimonthly report around 22 March could instead propose a change.

Markets already treat the post-run-off fiscal path as at risk. USD/BRL rose 7.61% in the week to 30 October, and the DI Jan-29 proxy rose from 12.81% to 14.86%. This cuts both ways. It raises the chance that fiscal looseness is the plan. It also gives the finance team a strong reason to defend the formal target in the short run, as the BCB's FX swap rollovers show officials managing stress rather than adding to it.

ai.what_would_change_view: I would move down if the December PLOA or LDO vote changes the 2027 target, or if a PLP is floated to alter the LC 200/2023 limits. I would also move down if the January finance-minister pick signals a framework rewrite, or if ministers publicly question the 0.5% target. I would move up if the PLOA passes in December without new exclusions and the Focus 2027 primary median moves toward the target.
ai.most_likely_wrong: The crowd's error may be treating 'will miss the target' as the same as 'will change the target'. Focus and IFI forecasts measure the first; this question resolves on the second, which is one reason I stay above even odds. My most likely error runs the other way: the LDO 2027 may still be open in Congress during the December budget session. That would let the target be lowered quietly by amendment before the window even starts in earnest, which my April-timing argument does not cover.

ai.base_rate_used: The scenario page has no direct base rate for keeping two-thirds. Its reference class (Mexico's midterms in 2009, 2015 and 2021) says only that the final-poll leader won 3 of 3, with an RMS poll error of 4.12 pp. The closest precedent is 2021, when the governing coalition kept its majority but lost two-thirds. My starting point is that a midterm usually trims the governing bloc and that holding 334 of 500 seats is the harder outcome. That puts the start somewhat below even.

factors.text: Reference-class pull downward: in the one recent midterm of a dominant governing coalition (2021) it kept its majority but lost two-thirds. The page's signpost says two-thirds needs roughly 55% of the vote plus the over-representation cap, a high bar to clear twice in a row.

Morena's dominance is not in doubt: Polymarket gives it 86.6% and Kalshi 86% to win the most seats. In 2024 Sheinbaum beat her 17 pp poll lead by winning by 33 pp, so polls have recently understated this coalition. But these markets are related-only (most seats, not two-thirds), and prediction-market gauges are tested_no_lead, so they get little weight.

The vote is seven months away, and the page notes poll errors are larger that far out than the 4.12 pp final-poll figure. The seat count also depends on INE's over-representation rulings, which a headline poll margin cannot capture (em-macro's 2024 lesson). That widens the spread of outcomes rather than shifting the centre.

ai.what_would_change_view: I would move up if early-2027 polls put the coalition's vote share above 55%, or if INE signals it will apply over-representation as leniently as in 2024. I would move down if PAN-PRI or MC form district alliances, or if coalition polling falls into the 45-55% band. The crowd's likely shared error is reading the 86.6% 'most seats' price as confidence in two-thirds. Those are different questions, and the gap between them is where the market risk sits (the 2024 peso fell sharply on the supermajority, not the presidency).
ai.most_likely_wrong: Sheinbaum's popularity and a fragmented opposition could repeat 2024. The coalition's vote share and INE's seat formula could then deliver two-thirds comfortably, as when polls understated Morena's margin by a wide amount in 2024.

ai.base_rate_used: The scenario page has no computed base rate: this is the agreement's first review cycle and em-macro has no trade-agreement events. I start from the nearest market price, Polymarket's 8.5% for an extension in 2026 (pm:2761052). That market covers the earlier review, not this question. The scenario's own event note implies the 2026 review ended without an extension. I then widen the starting point for the extra time to 1 July 2027.

factors.text: At the first chance to extend, in 2026, the crowd gave only 8.5% to an extension. The default under art. 34.7 is a cycle of annual reviews, so the US keeps the review as standing leverage. YES needs all three governments to confirm in writing, which is a high bar, and the default favours the annual branch.

Kalshi gives 24% to a trilateral revised deal in 2026. A revised text is the most natural vehicle for an extension, and recent USTR releases show the US and Mexico settling disputes cooperatively (Rapid Response labour case, Minera Peñasquito remediation). That keeps extension a live path rather than a tail.

US trade decisions often arrive off-calendar. Mexico's June 2027 midterms fall just before the 1 July review, and Morena's possible supermajority is itself a US concern. Both give Washington reasons to hold back a 16-year commitment until after the vote.

ai.what_would_change_view: I would move up if USTR's consultation report recommends extension, if US tariffs on Mexican goods are cut below 10%, or if a trilateral revised text is signed. Any of these would make a written confirmation by 1 July 2027 plausible. I would move down toward the bilateral or withdrawal branches if the US proposes separate US-Mexico and US-Canada texts, or if officials describe withdrawal as leverage. A collapse of the next US-Mexico bilateral round (placeholder date 30 November) would also push me down.
ai.most_likely_wrong: A political deal arrives as a package: tariff relief plus a revised text, signed with a 16-year extension before the US 2028 cycle. In that case thin, related-only markets and my status-quo default understate how quickly an extension can be granted once the US has extracted concessions.

calculator.name: USD/MXN

degraded.effect: Same Banxico series IDs, read from the public chart endpoint that backs banxico.org.mx graphs. It is unofficial and undocumented, so it can change without notice, and it serves the latest values only as of the page cache (can lag the API by hours).
degraded.upgrade: add the BANXICO_TOKEN secret under Settings > Secrets and variables > Actions; the next data run uses it and every feature switches over by itself

calculator.default_basis: today's level plus the expected move of the good and bad branches

notes: Moves marked assumption are judgements or rescalings, not em-macro estimates.
Market probabilities are hidden until you reveal them, as elsewhere on the site.
